clue.text: Lawrence's jumper

parts.note: D. H. Lawrence wrote an Australian novel named after a leaping marsupial, and that animal is a famous jumper

explanation.definitionFit: The title of Lawrence's 1923 novel is also the name of the hopping Australian animal, a natural jumper.

clue.text: He staged La Pucelle as a lark

definitions.text: He staged La Pucelle as a lark

parts.words: He staged La Pucelle as a lark
parts.note: La Pucelle is Joan of Arc; the French dramatist put her story on stage in the play L'Alouette, which means The Lark

explanation.surface: Someone mounted a play about Joan of Arc purely for fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As a lark' seems to mean 'for a joke', but it is the play's title, L'Alouette (The Lark), from 1952.
explanation.definitionFit: The French playwright wrote L'Alouette, a drama about Joan of Arc, known as La Pucelle (the Maid).

clue.text: Fiend which is cat, we hear

definitions.text: Fiend which is cat, we hear

parts.words: Fiend which is cat, we hear
parts.note: in Macbeth the first witch calls to her familiar spirit, a cat, by this name, so we hear of it as a fiend in feline shape

explanation.surface: Rumour has it that some demon is really a cat.
explanation.walkthrough: In Macbeth the first witch says 'I come, Graymalkin!', calling her familiar spirit; the name came to mean an old she-cat.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names an old female cat, and in Macbeth a witch's familiar spirit, a demon in feline form.

clue.text: State of Robert Tressell's benevolent character's slacks

definitions.text: State of Robert Tressell's benevolent character's slacks

parts.words: State of Robert Tressell's benevolent character's slacks
parts.note: Tressell's novel is The ___ Trousered Philanthropists: a philanthropist is a benevolent character and trousers are slacks

explanation.surface: A question about what condition a kindly man's trousers were in.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Tressell's 1914 novel is The Ragged Trousered Philanthropists, about house painters in an English town.
explanation.definitionFit: Tattered and torn describes the trousers in the title of Tressell's novel about poor workers.

clue.text: Errant undutiful roamer at length inherits in Victorian novel

indicators.note: errant means wandering astray, so the letters of the next two words stray into a new order

explanation.surface: A wayward, careless wanderer finally comes into an inheritance in a nineteenth-century story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Errant' rearranges UNDUTIFUL ROAMER. The words 'at length inherits' play on the plot, in which John Harmon finally comes into his inheritance.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's last completed novel, published 1864-65, during Queen Victoria's reign.

clue.text: LeRoi Jones presented that of Inferno

definitions.text: LeRoi Jones presented that of Inferno

parts.words: LeRoi Jones presented that of Inferno
parts.note: LeRoi Jones (later Amiri Baraka) wrote the novel The ___ of Dante's Hell, and Dante's Hell is his Inferno

explanation.surface: An American writer once set out the workings of Hell.
explanation.definitionFit: LeRoi Jones's 1965 novel is The System of Dante's Hell, Dante's Inferno being his Hell.

clue.text: Cowper's was passing sweet, Marvell's delicious

definitions.text: Cowper's was passing sweet, Marvell's delicious

parts.words: Cowper's was passing sweet, Marvell's delicious
parts.note: Cowper wrote 'How sweet, how passing sweet' of being alone, and Marvell in The Garden called it delicious

explanation.surface: Two poets compare something they each found sweet or delicious.
explanation.walkthrough: Cowper's Retirement has 'How sweet, how passing sweet, is solitude!'; Marvell's The Garden has 'Society is all but rude, To this delicious solitude.'
explanation.definitionFit: Both poets praised being alone, Cowper calling it passing sweet and Marvell delicious.

clue.text: As inconsequential as Cary's ballads

parts.note: the word for unimportant is also the title word of a collection of verses by the poet Cary

explanation.surface: Someone judges a poet's ballads to be of no importance.
explanation.definitionFit: Petty or unimportant matters are inconsequential, and the same word heads Cary's collection of light verse.

clue.text: Fellow's area of expertise is New Zealand writer

parts.note: a fellow is a man, and the 's adds an S
a field is a specialist area, as in 'it's not my field'

explanation.surface: A man's speciality turns out to be a writer from New Zealand.
explanation.walkthrough: Katherine Mansfield was a New Zealand short-story writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Katherine Mansfield, the short-story writer, was born in Wellington, New Zealand.

clue.text: Green's excessive fondness

parts.note: Henry Green wrote a 1952 novel whose one-word title means being foolishly fond

explanation.definitionFit: Henry Green's novel takes its title from the word for lavishing too much affection.

clue.text: Huxley offered it without revelation

parts.note: Julian Huxley's 1927 book was titled ___ without Revelation, a faith with no divine disclosure

explanation.surface: A Huxley put forward something but revealed nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without revelation' seems to mean 'without disclosing anything'; it is the end of Julian Huxley's book title, Religion without Revelation.
explanation.definitionFit: Julian Huxley's humanist book proposed a faith system that did without divine disclosure.

clue.text: Revolutionary sort of underground station?

definitions.meaning: the Comte de ... was a leading figure in the early French Revolution
a Paris Métro station bears the same name, so it is one kind of underground stop

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a rebel is a type of Tube station.
explanation.definitionFit: The French statesman of 1789 gives his name to a Paris Métro station and bridge.

clue.text: Thanks to a series of chords in pricelist

parts.note: ta is informal British for thank you
a riff is a short repeated musical phrase

explanation.surface: Gratitude for some chords turns up in a list of charges.
explanation.definitionFit: A table of charges or duties is a list of what things cost.

clue.text: He was a dramatist of note (as H. C. Bunner wrote)

definitions.text: He was a dramatist of note (as H. C. Bunner wrote)

parts.words: He was a dramatist of note (as H. C. Bunner wrote)
parts.note: H. C. Bunner's comic verse shortened ... name to its first syllable, and the word also means a trill, a musical note

explanation.surface: An American humorist describes a famous playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: H. C. Bunner's humorous poem 'Shake, Mulleary and Go-ethe' clips Shakespeare's name; 'of note' also hints at the musical trill.
explanation.definitionFit: Bunner's verse clipped Shakespeare's name to one syllable, which is also a trill in music.

clue.text: Greek poet reveals a date in Rome with simple chap

parts.note: Simple Simon is the nursery-rhyme simpleton
the ides were a fixed day in each month of the Roman calendar

explanation.surface: A Greek poet goes on a Roman date with a simpleton.
explanation.definitionFit: Simonides of Ceos was a lyric poet of ancient Greece, famous for epitaphs.

clue.text: Alice said it was a very interesting dance

definitions.text: Alice said it was a very interesting dance

parts.words: Alice said it was a very interesting dance
parts.note: in Wonderland the Mock Turtle and Gryphon perform the Lobster dance, and Alice politely calls it very interesting

explanation.surface: A girl comments that some dance was fascinating.
explanation.walkthrough: In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, after the Lobster Quadrille Alice says 'Thank you, it's a very interesting dance to watch.'
explanation.definitionFit: A square dance for four couples, made famous in Wonderland by the lobsters.

clue.text: "If those streams of hair were — in battle, I know nothing they were adapted to" (Horace Walpole)

definitions.text: "If those streams of hair were — in battle, I know nothing they were adapted to" (Horace Walpole)

parts.words: "If those streams of hair were — in battle, I know nothing they were adapted to" (Horace Walpole)
parts.note: the missing word in Walpole's sentence is a verb meaning to inconvenience or hamper

explanation.surface: A quotation from Horace Walpole with a word left out.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb means to trouble or get in someone's way, as long hair would in a fight.

clue.text: Egyptian lady-in-waiting to enchant Mr McEwan

parts.note: to charm someone is to enchant them
Ian McEwan is the English novelist

explanation.surface: An Egyptian attendant sets out to bewitch the novelist McEwan.
explanation.walkthrough: Charmian attends Cleopatra in Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra.
explanation.definitionFit: In Antony and Cleopatra, Charmian is one of the queen's attendants.

clue.text: In the intervening period of H. G. Wells

definitions.meaning: in the meantime, while something else goes on
Wells wrote a 1927 novel with this one-word title

explanation.surface: Something happened during a stretch of time in H. G. Wells's life.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means in the meantime, and Wells used it as a novel title in 1927.

clue.text: Rue meal badly cooked for cousin of Richard I

indicators.note: food cooked badly is messed up, so the letters of the two words are mixed up

explanation.surface: A rough meal is spoiled when prepared for a royal relative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly cooked' rearranges RUE MEAL. Aumerle is cousin to Richard II in Shakespeare's play; the printed 'Richard I' has probably lost an I.
explanation.definitionFit: The Duke of Aumerle appears as the king's kinsman and loyal supporter in Shakespeare's Richard II.

clue.text: "I just put my two arms round her, and said 'Come, Bessie! Don't—'." (Jane Eyre)

definitions.text: "I just put my two arms round her, and said 'Come, Bessie! Don't—'." (Jane Eyre)

parts.words: "I just put my two arms round her, and said 'Come, Bessie! Don't—'." (Jane Eyre)
parts.note: the missing word in Jane's plea to the nurse is a verb meaning to tell someone off

explanation.surface: A line from Jane Eyre with its last word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane asks Bessie not to reprimand her, the missing verb meaning to rebuke.

clue.text: Money church offered for victim of Tarquinius

parts.note: lucre is money, especially ill-gotten
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Cash is given to a church for a man's victim.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's The Rape of Lucrece tells of Lucretia, violated by Sextus Tarquinius.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's narrative poem the Roman matron Lucretia is assaulted by Tarquin's son.

clue.text: I phone about five to reach actor-manager

indicators.note: about means going round, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: to ring someone is to phone them
V is the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: Someone phones around five to get hold of a theatre boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' puts V inside RING. Sir Henry Irving was the great Victorian actor-manager of the Lyceum Theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Henry Irving ran the Lyceum Theatre in London and starred in its productions.

clue.text: Feeling less, like the one of Don Passos?

definitions.text: like the one of Don Passos?
definitions.meaning: Dos Passos wrote the novel ___ One, so the title's first word fits

explanation.surface: Someone feels less, like a character from Dos Passos.
explanation.walkthrough: John Dos Passos's novel Number One (1943) is about a demagogue; 'Don' is likely a misprint of 'Dos'.
explanation.definitionFit: More numb means having less feeling; and Dos Passos's political novel is Number One.

clue.text: Some war with—- — for their leathern wings " (A Midsummer Night's Dream)

definitions.text: Some war with—- — for their leathern wings " (A Midsummer Night's Dream)

parts.words: Some war with—- — for their leathern wings " (A Midsummer Night's Dream)
parts.note: Titania orders her fairies to fight creatures with leathery wings, an old word for bats

explanation.surface: A line from Titania's speech with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Titania says 'Some war with rere-mice for their leathern wings, To make my small elves coats.' Rere-mice are bats.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word for bats, whose leathery wings Titania wants for her elves' coats.

clue.text: Character of lampoon

parts.note: the nature of a satirical attack is mocking and scornful

explanation.definitionFit: A lampoon mocks its target, so its character is scornful and mocking.

clue.text: Posthumous marriage created difficulties for her

definitions.text: Posthumous marriage created difficulties for her

parts.words: Posthumous marriage created difficulties for her
parts.note: in Cymbeline the king's daughter secretly marries Posthumus Leonatus, which brings her great trouble

explanation.surface: A marriage made after death caused a woman trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Posthumous' seems to mean 'after death', but it is Posthumus, husband of Cymbeline's daughter Imogen.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's heroine in Cymbeline weds Posthumus against her father's will and suffers for it.

clue.text: "Where the King rides a bicycle" in some books we'd enjoy

definitions.text: Where the King rides a bicycle

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A line about a cycling king turns up in books we would like.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted phrase recalls the Scandinavian monarchy known for its unpretentious king, seen riding a bicycle.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scandinavian kingdom whose monarch was famously seen cycling in public.

clue.text: Bank on the Spanish verse

parts.note: Dogger Bank is a sandbank in the North Sea
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: Someone relies on a Spanish poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank on' looks like 'rely on'; it is Dogger Bank, a shipping-forecast area in the North Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Doggerel is poor, clumsy rhyme, a kind of poetry.
